hints: Trace the electrical wave in order. It starts at the sinoatrial node, spreads over the atria, then reaches the AVN sitting between the atria and ventricles. Ask yourself what needs to happen before the ventricles fire.
Think about timing for blood flow. The atria must finish contracting to push blood into the ventricles first, so which structure provides that short pause of about 0.1 s?
walkthrough:
**Recall the conduction pathway**

Great start, let us map it together. The sinoatrial node (SAN) fires, the wave spreads across the atria causing atrial systole, then it arrives at the atrioventricular node (AVN).

Pathway:
$$SAN \rightarrow atria \rightarrow AVN \rightarrow bundle \ of \ His \rightarrow Purkyne \ tissue \rightarrow ventricles$$

**Understand why a pause is needed**

Think like the heart. If ventricles contracted at the same time as atria, blood would not have time to move down into the ventricles. The AVN holds the wave briefly so the atria can fully empty.

**Choose the best description**

So the AVN does not start the heartbeat and does not block conduction completely. It simply delays transmission from the SAN to give that vital filling time. That matches option B perfectly.

options.A: This is the job of the SAN wave spreading across the atrial walls, not the AVN. The AVN receives the wave after the atria are already contracting.
options.B: Exactly right. The AVN imposes a short delay after SAN excitation so the atria finish contracting and the ventricles fill before ventricular systole.
options.C: The AVN does not act as a pacemaker to initiate a new wave. It passes on the original SAN wave to the bundle of His after the delay.
options.D: The non-conducting barrier is the layer of fibrous connective tissue between atria and ventricles. The AVN is conducting tissue, it is the only electrical link through that barrier.
